name: MathlibAnnex.WeakGradient.localMollification_fderiv_apply
title: Differentiating a local mollification through its kernel

content.display_title: Differentiating a local mollification through its kernel
content.one_sentence_role: Writes a directional derivative without differentiating the locally integrable input.
content.natural_language_statement:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed vector space with its Borel measurable structure and an additive Haar measure $\mu$. Fix $R>0$. For $k\in\mathbb N$, let $\varphi_k:E\to\mathbb R$ be the normalized smooth bump centered at zero with inner and outer radii
$$a_k=\frac{R}{2(k+2)},\qquad r_k=\frac{R}{k+2}.$$
It is nonnegative, has integral one, and has compact support in $\overline B(0,r_k)$. If $v:E\to\mathbb R$ is locally integrable, put
$$v_k(y):=(\varphi_k*v)(y)=\int_E\varphi_k(t)v(y-t)\,d\mu(t).$$
Then, for every $k$, $y\in E$, and direction $e\in E$,
$$Dv_k(y)e=\int_Ev(z)\,D\varphi_k(y-z)e\,d\mu(z).$$
content.assumptions: Only local integrability of $v$ is assumed. The theorem does not require a weak equation, global integrability, Lipschitz continuity, or differentiability of $v$. The dimension may be zero. The kernel is the specified normalized bump for these radii; no extra scaling formula for a universal kernel is assumed.
content.conclusion: The derivative is a genuine Fréchet derivative of the mollification, and the displayed scalar integral is integrable. Differentiation falls on the smooth compactly supported kernel, not on $v$.
content.proof_summary: Apply the compact-kernel differentiation theorem for convolution, evaluate its operator-valued integral in direction $e$, and change variables by the Haar-measure-preserving reflection $t=y-z$.

proof_steps.text:
**Apply the derivative theorem with its hypotheses.** The normalized bump $\varphi_k$ is $C^1$ and compactly supported, while $v$ is locally integrable on all of $E$. The [compact-kernel convolution differentiation theorem](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/360da6fa66c1273b76b6b2d8c5666fd5ac2e3b56/Mathlib/Analysis/Calculus/ContDiff/Convolution.lean#L93-L97) therefore yields
$$Dv_k(y)=\int_E v(y-t)\,D\varphi_k(t)\,d\mu(t).$$
This is an integral of continuous linear functionals on $E$. The derivative $D\varphi_k$ is continuous and compactly supported. Multiplication against the locally integrable translate of $v$ is therefore integrable, which justifies this operator-valued integral.

**Evaluate and change variables.** Evaluation $L\mapsto L(e)$ is continuous linear, so it commutes with that integrable Bochner integral:
$$Dv_k(y)e=\int_Ev(y-t)\,D\varphi_k(t)e\,d\mu(t).$$
Translation and negation preserve additive Haar measure on the real vector space. Thus the measurable bijection $z\mapsto y-z$, its own inverse, permits substitution $t=y-z$. Since $y-(y-z)=z$, the preceding formula becomes
$$Dv_k(y)e=\int_Ev(z)\,D\varphi_k(y-z)e\,d\mu(z).$$
No derivative of $v$ has been used.

content.lean_realization_notes: In the local application, $v=\mathbf1_Ku$ with $K$ compact and contained in an open set on which $u$ is locally integrable. Local integrability gives $\int_K|u|\,d\mu<\infty$, and measurability of compact $K$ gives integrability of $\mathbf1_Ku$ on $E$, hence the hypothesis of this theorem. Separately, the rank-one trace identity $\operatorname{tr}(z\mapsto L(z)e)=L(e)$ explains why the same directional kernel derivative occurs in the divergence test used later; it is not an assumption on $v$.
